catalog_quote: Kafoa has lexicalized stress. There is a common, but unpredictable, tendency for heavy syllables to bear stress. There is also a strong tendency for prefixes to bear stress. In unaffixed words there is a tendency for stress to appear on the first syllable. However, this is only a tendency, as stress is lexicalized in unaffixed words containing only light syllables, as evidenced by the data in Table 5. Table 5: Stress placement in words containing only light syllables Stressed 1st syllable Stressed 2nd syllable /'.po/ 'fruit' /i'ro/ 'egg' /'mo.ra/ 'afraid' /ta'ki ... primary stress may fall on either the first syllable or second syllable. Primary stress placement in tri ... heavy syllables to bear primary stress in disyllabic words. However, as with light syllables these are tendencies only, as illustrated in Table 6, which shows that stress is also lexicalized in words containing heavy syllables. Table 6: Stress placement in words with heavy syllables Stressed heavy syllable Unstressed heavy syllable /bu'rel/ 'worm' /'lo.lon ... Primary stress typically falls on the possessive prefix on possessed nouns, and the person prefixes and valency increasing prefixes on verbs. For example: stress falls on the possessive prefix ta- '1PL.INCL.INAL ... root word then primary stress tends to fall on the heavy syllable. Once again this is a tendency only.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Kafoa is lexically specified, not fixed: it must be learned per word. Statistical tendencies only: heavy syllables (long vowel, diphthong or coda) attract stress; unaffixed words tend to be stressed on the first syllable; but minimal-type contrasts exist among all-light words (/'mo.ra/ 'afraid' vs /i'ro/ 'egg') and among words with heavy syllables (/bu'rel/ 'worm' vs /'lo.lon-/). Morphology interacts: possessive prefixes on nouns and person/valency-increasing prefixes (incl. the u- applicative) on verbs typically carry primary stress; otherwise stress in the corpus fell on the first syllable of the root, or tends toward a heavy root syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned: when a prefix takes primary stress a heavy root syllable takes secondary stress (e.g. /'we.la/ 'bathe' -> prefixed /'ga.we.la/ 'wash him/her' with secondary stress on we:); in compounds the first member carries primary stress and the second is unstressed or carries secondary stress (sec. 2.6.2).
new_statements.exceptions: All placement statements are explicitly 'tendencies only'; Tables 5 and 6 list lexical counter-examples (2nd-syllable stress in all-light words; unstressed heavy syllables). Verbs with the u- applicative take primary stress on the applicative rather than the root-initial syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/corpus forms (author's field corpus, Probur area); distinction drawn between unaffixed words, prefixed words and compounds; Baird calls the system 'lexicalized', i.e. weakly contrastive/unpredictable rather than rule-governed. Full page text of p.65-66 (incl. complete Tables 5-6) was not viewable -- statement assembled from overlapping verbatim search snippets that agree word-for-word.
new_statements.identity_note: Baird's sketch describes Kafoa (speakers' own name Jafoo is not used in the sources seen) as spoken around Probur / Habollat, Desa Probur Utara, Kecamatan Alor Barat Daya, West Alor -- the single variety under Glottolog kafo1240 / ISO kpu; no dialect split is reported. 'Patji 2014' (Wikipedia, Schapper 2020) and 'Humaedi dkk. 2014' are the same LIPI Press volume. Google Books vol. id sWVCDwAAQBAJ is TAP Volume 2 (2017), not vol. 3, despite its introduction sharing stress-survey wording with Schapper 2020.

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2020. Introduction to The Papuan languages of Timor, Alor and Pantar, Volume 3, 1-52. De Gruyter Mouton (HAL author version). Sec. 5.1 Phonology.
sources.note: Family survey: AP languages have non-phonemic and weakly phonemic stress systems; 'phonemic stress systems bearing low functional loads' with stress on heavy syllables and lexicalized stress in all-light disyllables are widespread (Nedebang, Teiwa, Kamang, Sawila named). Kafoa is not named in the stress passage.

sources.citation: Stokhof, W. A. L. 1975. Preliminary notes on the Alor and Pantar languages (East Indonesia). Pacific Linguistics B-43. Canberra: ANU. Kafoa: language note p.12; wordlist no. 22 'Kafoa' pp.50-51; transcription key p.3.
sources.note: No prose rule. The 117-item Kafoa wordlist marks 'the relative prominence of that vowel' with an apostrophe before the vowel (key p.3); prominence in the list falls variously on penult, final and initial vowels (e.g. hiy'aka, tal'ama, kaf'uka vs ir'ow, mah'el, him'or vs 'uru, n'amih), i.e. raw data consistent with non-fixed stress.
